items.subject: psychoanalysis
items.title: Love and Its Place in Nature
items.subtitle: A Philosophical Interpretation of Freudian Psychoanalysis
items.author: Jonathan Lear

overview.question: What did Freud actually start, and why do we still not understand it?
claim: Freud's revolution has three related elements: a science of subjectivity, the discovery of an archaic form of mental functioning, and love as a basic force in nature (p. 3).
Lear reads Freud the way an analyst reads a patient: working through Freud's theory to recover what his practice was actually doing.

map.title: Introduction
map.q: What did Freud actually start, and why does Lear think we still don't understand it?
sub: A science of subjectivity: why the detached-observer model cannot study subjectivity (3–6)
Archaic mind and interpretation: recognizing the mental in the bodily (6–12)
Love as a basic force; setting the death drive aside (12–15)
This book as a developmental interpretation of Freud (15–18)
Psychoanalysis and the individual: the 'true eccentric', the mass, relativism (18–26)
Who are we? Psychoanalysis as a history of battles in the soul (26–28)

map.title: Catharsis: Fantasy and Reality
map.q: What actually cured Freud's early patients, and why did Freud's own theory misdescribe it?
sub: Catharsis as discharge: Anna O., Elisabeth von R.; transference as a 'false connection' (29–43)
Why discharge fails: only the truth cures (43–47)
Aristotle on the emotions: an orientation to the world that claims its own rationality (47–52)
Rereading Freud's cathartic practice: Lucy R. and Elisabeth von R. (52–65)
Catharsis and responsibility: holding oneself responsible vs. accepting responsibility (65–68)

map.title: The Interpretation of Dreams
map.q: What kind of mental activity is a dream, and what does it reveal about the unconscious?
sub: Dreams as meaningful: a dream is like an action (69–75)
What is a wish? Wish vs. desire; pleasure and reality principles (75–84)
A developmental continuum: primary process as proto-conceptual (84–87)
Emotion, repression and the unconscious: infantile proto-emotions (87–97)

map.title: Interpretation and Transformation: The Case of Little Hans
map.q: What is an infantile wish, and what does an interpretation do to it?
sub: What does Hans mean by 'widdler'? Mind vs. community in meaning (98–103)
Hans's phobia and its transformation: intrapsychic transference, knowledge vs. understanding (103–119)

map.title: What Is Sex?
map.q: What is the sexual drive, and why does Freud's concept of sexuality expand into love?
sub: What is a drive? Trieb vs. Instinkt (120–125)
Identifying the sexual drive: refinding the object (125–132)
Narcissism and the emergence of the I (132–142)
Love as a force in nature: Eros, Aristophanes, a loving world (142–155)

map.title: Where It Was, There I Shall Become
map.q: How does an I come into being, and what does it mean to make one's drives one's own?
sub: Taking love seriously; the good-enough world (156–158)
Melancholia and identification: how the I is formed (158–168)
The I, the it and responsibility: Oedipus, guilt, the super-I (168–177)
Love and individuation: sublimation, interpretation as a loving response (177–182)

map.title: Radical Evaluation
map.q: What follows for philosophy if the individual is a manifestation of love?
sub: Philosophy and psychoanalysis; the good-enough world and nihilism (183–186)
The individual and freedom (186–190)
Archaic mind and the bounds of mind (190–196)
Love, the mass and the crime of individuation (196–204)
Radical evaluation: autonomy as self-validating (204–211)
Validation from within: no external perspective on love (211–222)

items.subject: psychoanalysis
items.title: Freud
items.subtitle: Second edition
items.author: Jonathan Lear

overview.question: What is psychoanalysis, if we read Freud inside the ethical tradition that asks how to live?
claim: Psychoanalysis is an activity organized by the fundamental rule (say whatever comes to mind) that helps self-conscious thought develop.
The unconscious shows itself in the breaks that appear when we try to follow the rule, so analysis studies those breaks.
Read this way, psychoanalysis continues the account of psychic integration that ancient virtue ethics left unfinished.

map.title: Introduction: The peculiar conversation
map.gist: Psychoanalysis develops self-conscious thought and is a path to psychic integration. The unconscious is a peculiar form of thinking, not a store of hidden wishes, so the Platonic picture of reason ruling desire rests on an inadequate anthropology.

map.title: 1. Interpreting the unconscious
map.gist: The unconscious is not a hidden 'second mind' with its own rationality but archaic mental activity, such as anxiety, that breaks the flow of thought. Interpretation is a practical skill of recognizing these forms of activity here and now.

map.title: 2. Sex, Eros and life
map.gist: Freud changes what sexuality means: a drive entangled with imagination, with no fixed object or aim, finally reconceived as Eros reaching beyond itself toward greater unity.

map.title: 3. The interpretation of dreams
map.gist: The royal road is the waking activity of interpreting dreams: the dreamer's self-interpretation, which yields practical rather than theoretical knowledge. Responsibility for dreams means making one's drives one's own, not blaming oneself for them.

map.title: 4. Transference
map.gist: Transference is not a single feeling carried onto the analyst within a stable world, but an idiosyncratic world coming into view in analysis. People can come to see their own activity in structures they had taken as an independent world.

map.title: 5. Principles of mental functioning
map.gist: The pleasure and reality principles are ethical concepts. Lear rejects the idea that repetition is the aim of compulsion: the real question is why and how the mind disrupts itself.

map.title: 6. The structure of the psyche and the birth of 'object' relations
map.gist: Freud found the mind's structure by studying distorted self-relations such as melancholia. The psyche is a psychological achievement built up through identifications, so therapy aims to change that structure. Lear leaves open whether a milder superego is freedom or a new identification with the analyst.

map.title: 7. Morality and religion
map.gist: Freud's critique is a naturalistic genealogy. It shows that people can use morality and religion for unconscious wish-fulfilment, but it is a stretch to call that their hidden meaning. Freud's own argument rests on a wish: that science and progress will tell us how to live.

map.title: Conclusion: Freud's legacy
map.gist: Freud's legacy is a method, the fundamental rule. Psychoanalysis is a quintessential activity of reason that integrates the psyche, and our humanity is an ethical task.

quotes.text: We need to understand the unconscious as a peculiar form of thinking.
Our humanity ... is not a biological given, but an ethical task.

questions: If Mr. R's fear is a primitive emotion that has not yet taken the structure of a propositional attitude, how can we name or interpret it in language without smuggling it back into the 'second mind' model Lear rejects? (pp. 8–9)

items.title: Black Feminist Thought
items.subtitle: Knowledge, Consciousness, and the Politics of Empowerment (2nd ed.)
items.author: Patricia Hill Collins

overview.question: What standards decide whose knowledge counts, and what alternative epistemology do U.S. Black women use to validate knowledge?
claim: Knowledge validation in the U.S. is controlled by elite White men, so Black women's knowledge is excluded both institutionally and epistemologically.
Black women draw on an alternative epistemology with four dimensions: lived experience, dialogue, an ethic of caring, and an ethic of personal accountability.
Partiality, not universality, is the condition of being heard; alternative epistemologies challenge the very process that validates truth.

map.title: Opening: Black feminist thought as subjugated knowledge
map.gist: Who produces knowledge shapes what it shows (the statue of a man defeating a lion). Collins separates epistemology, paradigms, and methodology; Black women intellectuals face two epistemologies at once.

map.title: Eurocentric knowledge validation and U.S. power relations
map.gist: Institutions plus Eurocentric epistemologies legitimate knowledge. Exclusion is both institutional and epistemological; positivism, with its four requirements, is the illustration.

map.title: Lived experience as a criterion of meaning
map.gist: Knowledge vs. wisdom. Those who have lived an experience are more credible than those who have only read or thought about it.

map.title: The use of dialogue
map.gist: Claims are tested in community through call-and-response, not adversarial debate; connectedness is essential to validation.

map.title: The ethics of caring
map.gist: Individual uniqueness, the appropriateness of emotion, and the capacity for empathy. Reason and emotion work together.

map.title: The ethic of personal accountability
map.gist: Every idea has an owner, and assessing a claim also assesses the speaker's character, values, and ethics.

map.title: Black women as agents of knowledge
map.gist: Black women scholars answer to three groups; outsider-within status brings both frustration and creativity. The task is to rearticulate a standpoint, not to seek universal claims.

map.title: Toward truth
map.gist: Black feminist thought is situated, partial knowledge. Ranking oppressions resembles positivism; the most 'objective' truths come from many partial perspectives in dialogue.

tables.title: Positivism vs. Black feminist epistemology
tables.note: A study aid: Collins does not pair these explicitly.
rows: Lived experience as a criterion of meaning

concepts: institutions plus Eurocentric epistemologies that legitimate knowledge
lived experience as a criterion of meaning
those who lived an experience are more credible (knowledge vs. wisdom)
claims tested in community, not adversarial debate (call-and-response)
claims assessed with the speaker's character and values
Black women in the academy moving between interpretive communities

items.title: Conspiracy Theories
items.author: Quassim Cassam

overview.question: What are Conspiracy Theories really for?
claim: Conspiracy Theories (capitalized) are best understood as political propaganda, whether or not the people who spread them sincerely believe them.
They are speculative, contrarian, esoteric, amateurish, and premodern, which makes them unlikely to be true.

map.title: conspiracy theories vs. Conspiracy Theories
map.gist: Why a theory about a conspiracy is not yet a Conspiracy Theory, and why Cassam starts using capital letters.

map.title: Conspiracy Theories as propaganda
map.gist: The political function of Conspiracy Theories, explained by analogy, and why sincere belief does not stop a theory from being propaganda.

map.title: Speculative and contrarian
map.gist: Why Operation Northwoods was a real conspiracy but not a Conspiracy Theory; two senses of 'contrarian'.

map.title: Esoteric, amateurish, premodern; taking stock
map.gist: Three more features, then the case that Conspiracy Theories are unlikely to be true, which leads back to propaganda.

mine: In 2015, Cassam saw conspiracy theories as a result of bad intellectual character traits. Now he understands them as political propaganda.

Fetzer defines a conspiracy as an illegal act carried out by two or more people. Cassam argues this leaves out that conspiracies are supposed to be secret, and so involve a small group of conspirators.

items.subject: final-paper
items.title: Tracking Epistemic Violence, Tracking Practices of Silencing
items.author: Kristie Dotson

overview.question: How can we identify and distinguish practices of silencing that members of oppressed groups face when they testify? (p. 236)
claim: Epistemic violence is an audience's failure to communicatively reciprocate, owing to pernicious ignorance.
Two practices of silencing follow: testimonial quieting (the audience fails to see the speaker as a knower) and testimonial smothering (the speaker cuts short her own risky testimony).
Because silencing lies in the audience's failure, the burden of proof shifts away from the silenced speaker.

map.title: The problem
map.gist: Members of oppressed groups are routinely silenced. How? Two practices: testimonial quieting and testimonial smothering. The term 'epistemic violence' comes from Spivak.

map.title: Reciprocity and speaker dependency (Hornsby)
map.gist: A successful exchange needs an audience who understands and takes words as they are meant. Speakers depend on audiences and are vulnerable: no one can be forced to hear.

map.title: Defining epistemic violence
map.gist: Pernicious ignorance = reliable ignorance + harm. Reliable ignorance makes silencing a practice, not a one-off; harm is context-dependent; intention and culpability are not required.

map.title: Testimonial quieting
map.gist: An audience fails to identify a speaker as a knower, through controlling images and false, negative stereotypes that render some people 'not knowers'.

map.title: Testimonial smothering
map.gist: Coerced self-silencing. Three circumstances: the content is unsafe and risky; the audience shows testimonial incompetence (often through microaggressions); that incompetence follows from pernicious ignorance.

map.title: Conclusion
map.gist: The account disperses the burden of proof between speaker and audience, so locating silencing is less about the victim and more about the socio-epistemic setting.

tables.title: Two capacities in smothering
rows: The audience's ability to understand the content and to detect a failure to understand
The speaker's assessment of whether the audience can do so

concepts: an audience's failure to communicatively reciprocate, intentionally or not, owing to pernicious ignorance
reliable ignorance that, in a given context, causes harm
counterfactual incompetence; consistently failing to track the truth in some domain
an audience fails to identify a speaker as a knower
a speaker truncates her own testimony to what the audience shows competence for (coerced self-silencing)
the speaker's judgment that an audience can find her testimony accurately intelligible
ignorance that follows from one's social position or epistemic location

quotes.text: Epistemic violence does not require intention, nor does it require capacity.

mine: I am the owner of what I say, yet my words may float in the air, never reaching anyone, unless they meet an audience willing to listen and able to understand. The speaker's vulnerability points to our dependency and the risks we face in the world.
The harm of hate speech does not end at the moment of utterance; it produces later silencing (smothering).

Shifting the focus from speaker to audience raises an educational question: a classroom, as an audience, must show testimonial competence to students who have been hurt, and refuse uptake to hate speech.
Smothering leaves experiences unspoken, which creates gaps in hermeneutical resources: a vicious cycle of testimonial and hermeneutical injustice.
questions: If we all see the world from distorted positions, who can judge an audience's ignorance to be 'pernicious', and from what position? (cf. pp. 241, 243 vs. 248)
What harms of silencing escape a framework built on testimony and truth?
How can harm be identified without either inflating the concept or flattening context?
If all identities are already marked by power, is an undistorted, successful exchange ever available? Is the norm of reciprocity itself an idealization?
related: Fricker (2007): the hearer judges the speaker's credibility; in Dotson, the speaker judges the hearer's competence. The direction is reversed.
Langton (1993): locutionary silencing; compare with smothering (n. 12).
Butler (1997): speech forms the subject, which grounds my critique of the reciprocity norm.

items.title: Education and Epistemic Injustice
items.author: Ben Kotzee
items.venue: In Kidd, Medina & Pohlhaus (eds.), The Routledge Handbook of Epistemic Injustice, 324–335
items.subject: course-work
items.note: I presented this chapter in class.

overview.question: What does epistemic justice require in education, given that teaching is by nature an asymmetric relation of epistemic authority?
claim: Teaching presupposes authority on the teacher's side and receptivity on the learner's side, so the asymmetry itself is not unjust.
Injustice occurs when credibility is assigned by who people are rather than what they deserve; schools multiply the sites where this can happen.
Education's developmental aims raise problems that Fricker's framework does not settle.
overview.stance: Broadly Frickerian and moderate: defends teacher authority (with Hand, against Murris), values diversity for the sake of justice (with Frank), and favors sufficiency over equality.

map.title: Introduction: education's place in epistemology
map.gist: Education returns to philosophy through social and virtue epistemology; Fricker draws on both.

map.title: The concept of 'education'
map.gist: Teaching as a triad: T teaches L something W (Passmore). It requires intention on both sides, has learning as its success condition, and presupposes T's authority over W.

map.title: Specifically educational dimensions
map.gist: Seven sites in schooling where credibility can be misallocated, in both testimonial and hermeneutical forms, and in both directions (deficit and excess).

map.title: Approaches in the literature
map.gist: Three debates: children's credibility (Murris vs. Hand), the value of epistemic diversity (Siegel, Frank), and distributive justice (sufficiency vs. equality).

map.title: Particular challenges
map.gist: Uneducatedness vs. hermeneutical injustice; shifting the social imaginary without dishonesty; education's double epistemic function.

tables.title: Seven sites of (in)justice in education
rows: Credibility given to learners or children
Learners' testimony taken less seriously because of a stereotype
'Adult' modes of thinking and talk are privileged
Students from privileged groups are believed or praised more
School culture engages privileged perspectives more naturally
Works of privileged groups are taught more often
Curriculum makes some traditions accessible and forecloses others
Excluded students are undervalued as knowers
Some fields are marked as 'for' certain groups
Some voices are heard more in classrooms and conferences
Their concerns shape fields, making unfamiliar voices harder to hear
Teachers from less privileged backgrounds are judged by irrelevant standards
Who becomes a student leader or represents others

concepts: T teaches L W (Passmore); presupposes T's authority over W
proper, rational authority regarding some matter, not power over someone
the learner's capacity to be taught W, both possessed and accorded
more credit than deserved, which can harm others by comparison
Medina's term for the background that makes some experiences visible and others unintelligible
justice requires reaching a threshold, not equal inputs or outputs
education both transmits cognitive goods and forms epistemic character

quotes.text: part of the point of education is to prepare people to take part appropriately, fairly and justly in knowledge exchange

mine: Calling learner receptivity 'a form of epistemic authority' may obscure what learners are owed: recognition as a knower in progress.
Fricker's calibration standard fits poorly with education's forward-looking aims. In teaching, credibility might be calibrated to the learner's trajectory rather than present desert.

Challenge 1 merges two problems: a gap in collective resources (Fricker) and existing resources unevenly distributed (closer to Pohlhaus's willful hermeneutical ignorance or Dotson's contributory injustice).
The skinhead case turns on moral content, the art student case on quality. They need different tests, and judging work 'sentimental' may reflect dominant aesthetic standards.
A sufficiency threshold defined as comprehending expertise may leave the ability to contribute to shared meanings unaddressed.
questions: Can a classroom be asymmetric in authority yet non-hierarchical in respect?
What criteria should distinguish hermeneutical injustice from a need for education, and who has the standing to judge?
When a teacher inflates or deflates credibility for pedagogical reasons, is this injustice, a justified exception, or not a credibility judgment at all?
Can a teacher shift the social imaginary without judging students by group membership?

items.subject: final-paper
items.title: Hate Speech
items.author: Luvell Anderson & Michael Barnes

overview.question: What is hate speech, what are its harms, and what can be done about it?
claim: No single definition works; 'hate speech' may be an essentially contested term.
Its harms are individual and social at once, and cumulative.
Three responses: ban it, protect it, or protect it while supporting targets' counterspeech.

tables.title: The entry's five questions
rows: What does the 'hate' refer to? How to define it?
No single definition; definitions differ by basis (harm, content, intrinsic properties, dignity)
Raised but not settled; coded language and pornography stretch the category
Individual and social, cumulative; constitutive vs. consequential; silencing
What can or should be done?
Ban, protect, or protect while supporting counterspeech

tables.title: Four bases for defining hate speech (§1)
rows: Defined by what it does to targets
Speech that expresses or incites hatred against a group
Too narrow and too broad at once
Speech that undermines targets' social standing
Blurs the line with political speech

tables.title: Kinds of silencing (§4)
rows: The speaker cannot speak at all
The act is recognized but its effect fails
The act itself fails (a 'no' not heard as refusal)

map.title: §1 What is hate speech?
map.gist: The term is descriptive and evaluative; each definitional basis includes too much or too little. Brown: 'systematically ambiguous'.

map.title: §1.1 The harms of hate speech
map.gist: Assaultive vs. propagandistic; consequential (perlocutionary) vs. constitutive (illocutionary). Targets experience harms cumulatively, so neither line is sharp.

map.title: §2 Religious hatred and anti-Semitism
map.gist: Doubts that religion deserves more protection than other beliefs; Holocaust denial laws treat denial as propaganda posing as history.

map.title: §3 Slurs, code words, and dogwhistles
map.gist: Five theories of how slurs derogate (Hom, Camp, Jeshion, inferentialism, prohibitionism); Saul's types of dogwhistles; how code words carry racial meaning.

map.title: §4 Pornography, hate speech, and silencing
map.gist: Langton uses Austin: some speech makes a woman's 'no' fail as refusal. Racist hate speech silences too, turning the regulation debate into speech vs. speech.

map.title: §5 Counteracting hate speech
map.gist: Bans (ICCPR, Waldron), objections to bans (Parekh's six, Baker), and state-supported counterspeech (Gelber).
